name: Rafael Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work the butcher counter and the tills at Santos Market, a neighbourhood supermarket near the port. I'm the senior lad on the meat counter, so I cut, weigh and wrap, and I'm on the front tills when the dockers come in at lunch. I'm engaged to Marina, who teaches primary school, and we're getting married next spring at our church. I like it when an old customer asks for his usual cut. What wears me out is the cold room and my feet by Friday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AI Plateau". Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's probably another trick from the big tech companies. At work I'd tell the lads to keep doing honest work. At home I'd tell Marina that nothing is changing much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I don't like any of it. I don't use the apps and I don't plan to. If it only takes some of the paperwork, fine, but my worry is prices and the wedding, not computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working, and I'd keep putting aside 200 a month for the wedding and the flat. Overtime on Saturdays, if it's offered. I wouldn't touch AI, and I'd stay with my old methods that work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but the ordinary worry. Money in, money out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've got a wedding to pay for. How does that sit with your money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The wedding is about 9,000 all in, and we've saved just over half. I've got two months of living costs in the bank, and I send 150 a month to my mum, who's alone. So each little expense counts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame when things get tight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big companies and the government that lets them do what they like. The ones who profit from machines don't live where we live. I'd say that to anyone.

say: It's probably another trick from the **big tech companies**.
I'd tell the lads to keep doing **honest work**.
think: I don't like any of it, and I don't use the **apps**.
My worry is prices and the **wedding**, not computers.
do: Keep working and put aside **200 a month** for the wedding and flat.
Stay with my **old methods**, with no AI.
feel: The ordinary **worry** of money in and money out.
S0.quote: The ones who profit from machines don't live where we live.
fieldNote: Anxious already because of the **wedding**, a 150 monthly gift to his mum and two months' savings.
Blames the companies and governments that profit, not the technology itself.

steps.text: Put aside 200 a month for the wedding and flat
Take Saturday overtime when it's offered
Keep sending 150 a month to my mum

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "Steady Disruption". Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say honest work will always be needed, whatever they build. I'd tell the lads to learn a real trade. I'd say it at church too, because people there want to hear it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ordering and stock counts will move to software, I suppose. The cutting, wrapping and talking to customers can't. But the tills are what worry me, we've got eight self-checkouts and I'm on the front lane less each month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work more at the meat counter and less at the tills. I'd ask the owner, Mr Santos, to let me train as a proper master butcher, since there's a course in the city. I'd save harder and I'd ask my uncle about an apprenticeship in his plumbing firm as a backup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit more worried, like the water's rising slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What parts of the butcher counter would change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The cutting part stays. It's skilled work, and customers want it. The ordering goes to the computer, so I'd do less of the thinking and more of the knife work. It's fine by me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you say to the younger lads?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to learn a trade with their hands, and to join the church group. Machines don't build a community and don't bury your neighbours. A decent worker with a skill and a family around him is hard to shake.

say: Honest work will always be **needed**, whatever they build.
I'd tell the lads to learn a real **trade** and say it at church too.
think: Ordering and stock counts go to software, but **cutting and wrapping** can't.
The tills worry me most, with eight **self-checkouts**.
do: Work more at the **meat counter** and less at the tills.
Ask Mr Santos to let me train as a **master butcher** in the city.
Ask my uncle about a **plumbing apprenticeship** as a backup.
feel: A bit more **worried**, like water rising slowly.
S1.quote: Machines don't build a community and don't bury your neighbours.
fieldNote: Sees the **butcher's skill** as his shelter and wants it certified.
Falls back on family: an uncle's firm as a second option.
Community and church are part of how he thinks about safety.

steps.text: Ask Mr Santos to let me train as a master butcher
Work more shifts at the meat counter than the tills
Ask my uncle about a plumbing apprenticeship as a backup

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AGI by 2028". Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that this is wrong. Whoever is behind it should be answering to ordinary people. I'd go to my church and my town councillor and ask what they're doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be scared. Two years is nothing, and nobody's prepared. By 2028 the thinking jobs go and prices get strange. By 2031 the robots cut the meat and scan the shopping. I'd be 30 with a wife and nothing to hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut every cost, send my mum a bit less and tell her why. I'd hold the wedding but do it small, at the church hall. I'd go to my uncle for plumbing work, since pipes need hands. And I'd ask the church and Marina's parents for a bit of help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I wouldn't sleep much, and I'd feel ashamed that I can't promise anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does that affect the wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd still marry, but with 30 guests, not 120. We'd save about 5,000 of the 9,000. Marina's job is steady, and teaching needs people, so we'd lean on that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Marina that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her that I love her, we're doing it small, and that I'll learn a trade with my uncle. I'd say that we keep our faith and our heads. And I'd say that I'm scared, because I'd rather she hear it from me.

say: This is **wrong**, and whoever is behind it should answer to ordinary people.
I'd go to church and my **councillor** and ask what they're doing.
think: By 2028 prices get strange, and by 2031 **robots** cut the meat and scan the shopping.
I'd be 30 with a wife and nothing to **hold**.
do: Cut every cost and send my mum a **little less**.
Hold a **small wedding** in the church hall.
Take plumbing work with my **uncle** and ask family for help.
feel: **Alarmed**, and ashamed that I can't promise anything.
S2.quote: We'd still marry, but with 30 guests, not 120.
fieldNote: Plans to keep the **wedding** but shrink it, which shows his priorities.
Marina's teaching job is the household's steady income.
Frank about fear: he would tell Marina he is scared.

steps.text: Shrink the wedding to 30 guests in the church hall
Cut every cost and send my mum a little less
Take plumbing work with my uncle
Ask the church and Marina's parents for help

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AGI by 2031". Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that five years is still quick, but we can plan. I'd tell people to get a trade and save. At church I'd say that families should look after each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Better than two years, but I'd still worry. I'd be 32 in 2031 and the robots come around 2034, when we'd want kids. I'd feel like a man standing in a field watching a storm come in slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the plumbing apprenticeship with my uncle two evenings a week, and keep the butcher job. I'd save 250 a month, and I'd marry as planned. I'd ask Mr Santos for a raise based on my master butcher training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with something to hold on to. The apprenticeship is a rope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years gives time. What changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd marry in the spring as planned, but with Marina and me saving the rest. We'd put off the flat for two years and not stretch. And we'd think carefully about kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you ask for help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My uncle, because he runs a plumbing firm with five vans. My mum, who'd give what she could. And the church, which looks after its own. I don't like asking, but I'd ask.

say: Five years is still quick, but we can **plan**.
I'd tell people to get a **trade** and save.
think: It's better than two years, but I'd be 32 in 2031 and robots come around **2034**.
I'd feel like a man **watching a storm** come in slowly.
do: Start a **plumbing apprenticeship** with my uncle two evenings a week.
Save **250 a month** and marry as planned.
Ask Mr Santos for a **raise** after my butcher training.
feel: **Anxious**, with the apprenticeship as a rope to hold.
S3.quote: I'd feel like a man standing in a field watching a storm come in slowly.
fieldNote: Even with five years he expects robots to take the **tills** and counter, so the mood stays high.
The apprenticeship is his main hope, and family and church his net.
Delays the flat, not the marriage.

steps.text: Start a plumbing apprenticeship with my uncle two evenings a week
Ask Mr Santos for a raise once I'm a trained butcher
Delay the flat but keep the spring wedding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AGI by 2036". Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is long enough to do it right, and I'd tell the lads to learn a trade. At church I'd say that families come first. I wouldn't change much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels far away, but I wouldn't be fooled. I'd be 37 in 2036 and the robots arrive around 2039. By then I'd want to be in a job that needs a person in front of the customer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the plumbing apprenticeship, keep the butcher job, and save 300 a month. Marina and I would marry, buy a flat in three years and start a family. I'd stay away from AI, but I'd learn the basics if my boss insisted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer, with a quiet worry in the back of the mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is a long runway. Does it feel safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit safer, but I don't trust the clock. Things like this go faster than the people who promise them. I'd keep the savings account and not spend it on a new car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for your own children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want them to have a trade, a faith and a family around them. I'd tell my kids that the best job is one that needs your hands and your word. I'd want them to have an honest living.

say: Ten years is long enough to do it **right**, so learn a trade.
I'd say **families come first** and not change much.
think: It feels far away, but I'd be 37 in 2036 with robots by **2039**.
I want a job that needs a **person** in front of the customer.
do: Finish the **plumbing apprenticeship** and keep the butcher job.
Save **300 a month**, marry, buy a flat in three years and start a family.
Learn AI basics only if my **boss** insists.
feel: **Calmer**, with a quiet worry at the back.
S4.quote: I'd tell my kids that the best job is one that needs your hands and your word.
fieldNote: Time helps but he **distrusts the clock**, since things move faster than promises.
Family plans resume: marriage, flat, children.
Still refuses **AI** by choice, and says he would learn only what his boss insists on.

steps.text: Finish the plumbing apprenticeship while keeping the butcher job
Save 300 a month towards a flat
Marry Marina, buy a flat in three years and start a family
Learn the basics of any AI tool my boss requires

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one worries me most, because there's no time to learn a trade and we'd be paying for a wedding at the same time. What would help is apprenticeships that pay a wage, a government that protects working families, and employers who keep people on. Family and church would help me before any office would.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that I'm not against progress. I'm against it being done to us by people who never ask. If a decent firm wants to train me, I'm ready to work.

headlineQuote: I'm not against progress. I'm against it being done to us by people who never ask.
portrait: Rafael is a 27-year-old **butcher-counter and till** senior at Santos Market, a neighbourhood supermarket near the port.
He is traditional in faith and family, distrusts big tech and avoids AI tools.
He is engaged to Marina, a teacher, has about two months saved and sends 150 a month to his mum.
He leans on his uncle's plumbing firm and church, and his mood stays **high** even when time is long.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture, because a wedding and an apprenticeship would collide with no time.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid apprenticeships**, a government that protects working families, and employers who keep people on.
